state.misconception_label: Assumes that an arrow on a number line starts at zero

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: I have: ![Number line with -12 and -7 marked. Starting at -12, follow an arrow pointing to the right labelled +10. Then there is an arrow labelled b pointing to the left, which ends at -7 on the number line.]() What is the value of \( b \) ? I got \( -7 \) because I'm not sure I worked it out the right way.

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Imagine you're on a hike, starting at -12 on a trail. You walk 10 steps to the right, then turn around and walk back 5 steps to the left. Where do you end up? Let's think about how the numbers on the number line represent this journey.

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: Oh right, so if I start at -12 and go right 10 steps, I'd be at -2, and then if I go left 5 steps I'd end up at -7... wait, is that what b is? So b would be -5, not -7?

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: That's right! Just like how you walked 10 steps to the right and then 5 steps back to the left on the hike, the same idea applies to the number line. So, if you start at -12 and go right 10 steps to -2, then go back 5 steps to the left, you end up at -5. Great job connecting the real-world situation to the number line!

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: Oh wait, I'm a bit confused now - you said I end up at -7 on the number line, but then you said b is -5? I thought b was supposed to be the arrow going left, so is b the number of steps I walk (-5) or is it something else?

score.justification_pass1: The teacher's analogy obscures rather than clarifies the misconception about arrow starting points, introduces a confusing error in Turn 3 (claiming the student ends at -5 when they should end at -7), and leaves the student more confused by the end as evidenced by Turn 4's legitimate question about what b represents.
score.justification_pass2: The teacher consistently uses a concrete hiking analogy to ground the abstract number line problem in an everyday physical experience, making the mathematical concept tangible through real-world movement.
